items.prompt: What is a reference architecture, most precisely?
choices: A documented blueprint for a recurring problem shape
One company's exact production system, copied as it stands
A mandatory standard that every team must follow
items.explanation: It is the distilled, reusable shape under many companies' versions of the same problem, not one specific system and not a rule.

items.prompt: Which of these names a broad architectural style rather than a sub-problem pattern?
choices: Saga pattern
Event-driven architecture
Strangler fig migration pattern
items.explanation: Event-driven describes how a whole system is organised. Saga and strangler fig each answer one specific recurring sub-problem.

items.prompt: A change in one system must reach other systems without ever being lost. Which catalogued pattern fits this shape?
choices: Transactional outbox with an event log
Pipe-and-filter chains of processing stages
Strangler fig gradual migration
items.explanation: The shape "tell others a state change happened, reliably" is exactly what the outbox with a durable log was written for.

items.prompt: One business step has to touch several services that share no database. Which pattern fits?
choices: Circuit breaker pattern
Saga with undo steps
Pipe-and-filter
items.explanation: Saga gives multi-step consistency without a distributed transaction by pairing each step with an undo.

items.prompt: A flaky downstream dependency keeps dragging its upstream callers down with it. Which pattern fits?
choices: Strangler fig, which shifts traffic slowly
Saga, which undoes steps
Circuit breaker, which fails fast
items.explanation: A circuit breaker fails fast instead of piling up timeouts, so one slow dependency does not exhaust everything upstream.

items.prompt: A legacy system must be replaced step by step, not in one cutover. Which pattern fits?
choices: Circuit breaker
Strangler fig
CQRS
items.explanation: Old and new run side by side while traffic shifts gradually, which is the strangler fig shape.

items.prompt: Data must move through several independent transformation steps that stay testable alone. Which pattern fits?
choices: Saga
Transactional outbox
Pipe-and-filter
items.explanation: Each stage is a filter with a defined input and output, so any stage can be tested or swapped by itself.

items.prompt: Can the same sub-problem pattern appear in both a layered monolith and a microservices system?
choices: Yes, because any style can contain that sub-problem
No, each pattern belongs to exactly one style of system
Only when both systems share one single database
items.explanation: Patterns and styles are independent choices; both kinds of system may need to notify consumers reliably.

items.prompt: A layered monolith and a microservices system both need to reliably notify downstream consumers. What does this show?
choices: The same catalogued pattern can serve either style
Both systems must first adopt one common style
Reliable notification only works with microservices
Each style needs its own freshly invented design
items.explanation: The notification problem is a sub-problem shape. It is independent of whether the surrounding system is layered or service-based.
items.reference:
Style versus pattern
🏛️ Style: the broad shape of a whole system (layered, event-driven)
🧩 Reference pattern: a named answer to one recurring sub-problem inside any style
🔎 Example sub-problem: "tell other systems a change happened, reliably"
Why: a style is chosen once for the whole system; a pattern is looked up each time a known problem shape appears inside it.
items.learnMore:
A pattern is a distilled shape, not a company

A reference architecture is the reusable shape underneath many versions of the same problem, with its known trade-offs and a diagram someone already tested in public. It does not replace the choice of broad style; it answers a smaller question inside whichever style you picked.

Common mistake

Treating "outbox" or "saga" as a whole-system style. They solve one sub-problem and sit inside a layered, event-driven or service-based system alike.
items.reflection: Think of a problem outside software (moving house, running a kitchen) where people have a named, repeatable way of doing one sub-task. What is the shape, and what would a beginner waste time re-inventing?

items.prompt: Which statement names a solution to a sub-problem, not a choice of whole-system style?
choices: "Our whole system is event-driven end to end"
"We use the outbox pattern for order changes"
"We chose a layered web application overall"
"Our services are organised as hexagonal modules"
items.explanation: The outbox is a specific answer to reliable notification. The other statements describe how a whole system is organised.

items.prompt: A team must retire an old billing system without a big-bang rewrite. Which description names the shape of that problem?
choices: Reads and writes needing structurally different models
Independent transformation stages passing data along
A dependency that has to fail fast when it is slow
Gradual replacement, old and new running side by side
items.explanation: The defining feature is incremental replacement of a legacy system, which is the strangler fig shape.

items.prompt: The opening team spent three sprints and ended with a design that already had a name. What did they pay for?
choices: A licence fee for a proprietary catalog entry of the pattern
Extra hardware to run a replay log
The full cost of discovering an already-solved shape
items.explanation: Nothing was wrong with the result; the cost was working it out from a blank page when the shape was already known.

items.prompt: Besides time, what second cost does the unit name for solving a known shape in isolation?
choices: Re-deriving failure modes, often in production
Paying an outside architect to approve the final design
Losing database choice
items.explanation: Catalog entries list failure modes such as duplicate delivery and retry storms; without them you learn each one by being hit.

items.prompt: What does a shared name such as "outbox pattern" buy a team?
choices: A guarantee that the resulting code is bug-free
Freedom from failure modes
A short label that a listener can look up
items.explanation: The name carries the shape and its trade-offs, so a new hire reads about it instead of needing a paragraph.

items.prompt: Is a catalog entry a rule saying you must implement it exactly one way?
choices: No, it is a starting point to adapt
Yes, any deviation makes it a different pattern
Only for cloud providers
items.explanation: Entries describe a class of problems; your own constraints still shape the final design.

items.prompt: According to the flow in L1, what comes right after "problem shows up"?
choices: Pick the most modern pattern you already know
Name the shape: what varies, what must hold
Draw the boxes of a custom design
items.explanation: Naming the shape is the step that lets you check a catalog before designing anything.

items.prompt: When is designing from first principles justified?
choices: When the catalog lookup shows the shape is novel
Whenever the team happens to have spare sprint time
Whenever a pattern name sounds too famous
items.explanation: Designing from scratch is fine once the lookup fails; the mistake is skipping the lookup.

items.prompt: Does using a reference architecture mean the team never thinks about failure modes?
choices: Yes, an entry covers every possible failure
No, it gives known ones but not your own
Yes, if the diagram is copied
items.explanation: The entry prices in the common mistakes. Your own constraints can still add new failure modes.

items.prompt: Which of these is a failure mode that a catalog entry for reliable notification would already list?
choices: A typo in some variable name inside one file
A slow laptop on the team
Duplicate delivery of one notification
items.explanation: Duplicates, ordering problems and retry storms are classic failure modes of notification designs and are documented.

items.prompt: A team handles duplicate delivery only after customers receive two emails. Which cost does this illustrate?
choices: Vocabulary loss: no shared name existed for the idea
Over-provisioning: building for far more consumers than needed
Style mismatch: choosing the wrong broad architecture overall
Rediscovery cost: meeting a listed failure mode the hard way
items.explanation: Duplicate delivery is a documented failure mode of this shape. Finding it in production is exactly the rediscovery cost.
items.reference:
What recognising the shape saves
🗓️ Without a catalog: blank page, rediscover retries, ordering, replay
⚠️ Failure modes found "the hard way", often in production
🗣️ With a catalog: a three-word name plus documented trade-offs
Why: a catalog entry is a documented starting point with the mistakes already priced in, so you adapt instead of rediscover.
items.learnMore:
Two costs stack up when a solved shape is solved again

The first is rediscovery: re-deriving duplicate delivery, out-of-order events and retry storms that an entry already lists. The second is lost vocabulary: a paragraph of explanation instead of a name a newcomer can go and read about.

Common mistake

Thinking a catalog entry is a rule to follow exactly. It is a starting point that you still adapt to your own constraints.
items.reflection: Recall a time you (or someone you know) spent days on something that already had a standard answer. What would naming the shape first have changed?

items.prompt: A new hire needs a paragraph to understand "we log state changes and replay them". What would a shared name have given?
choices: A short label they can look up and read
A guarantee of no bugs
A faster database for the replay step itself
Permission to skip reviewing the design at all
items.explanation: The saving is communication: three words that point to documented material instead of a retold explanation.

items.prompt: After checking catalogs, a team finds no entry matching their shape. What is the sound next step?
choices: Adopt the closest famous pattern unchanged, then patch the gaps later
Wait until a matching catalog entry gets published
Design from first principles, now justified by the lookup
Copy a competitor's design and skip the fit check
items.explanation: Designing from scratch is only a mistake when it replaces the lookup. After a failed lookup it is the right move.

items.prompt: Which signal points toward CQRS?
choices: A state change must reach other systems reliably
Reads outnumber writes and need another shape
A legacy system must be replaced gradually
items.explanation: CQRS pays off when read and write models need structurally different shapes, not merely different volumes.

items.prompt: Which signal points toward event sourcing?
choices: A dependency is occasionally slow, flaky or even completely down
Data passes through several transformation steps
State must be provably rebuilt from its full history
items.explanation: Event sourcing treats history as the primary fact and derives the current state from it.

items.prompt: Which signal points toward the saga pattern?
choices: Reads and writes need clearly different data shapes and indexes
One business step spans services with no shared database
Support staff only sometimes look at past values
items.explanation: A saga coordinates a multi-service business step through forward and compensating actions.

items.prompt: A report is slow. Is that alone enough to justify CQRS?
choices: Yes, slow reads always mean you need to adopt CQRS
Yes, but only if the report runs overnight
No, it is a symptom and may need only an index
items.explanation: CQRS addresses different read and write shapes. A slow query might be fixed by an index at almost no cost.

items.prompt: How does a history table treat the past, compared with event sourcing?
choices: As a byproduct of the present, kept in case
As the primary fact of the system
As something deleted again after every single update
items.explanation: A history table copies rows as a convenience. Event sourcing stores the changes and derives the state.

items.prompt: Which catalog is the best fit for messaging shapes such as dead-letter queues and content-based routers?
choices: Design Patterns by the Gang of Four, in object form
Any cloud provider's public pricing page
Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe and Woolf)
items.explanation: That book catalogs messaging patterns; the Gang of Four book covers finer-grained object shapes in code.

items.prompt: Where would you look first for a catalogued saga or circuit-breaker pattern?
choices: microservices.io, a public pattern catalog
Only inside a paid vendor training course
The standard library shipped with your language
items.explanation: It catalogs service-decomposition and distributed-system patterns, including saga, CQRS and circuit breaker.

items.prompt: What do cloud-provider reference architecture centers mainly offer?
choices: Language-level object patterns for single classes
End-to-end blueprints naming concrete managed services
Language-level object patterns for single classes and methods
items.explanation: They are whole-system blueprints with specific services, unlike pattern catalogs that stay vendor-neutral.

items.prompt: A slow report turns out to be caused by a missing index. Which conclusion is right?
choices: CQRS was needed after all, just a bit later on in the project
The report should get its own event-sourced model
It was a query-tuning problem, so no pattern was needed
A saga should coordinate the report queries
items.explanation: A symptom with a cheap local fix does not match any pattern signal. Adding CQRS would add a second model for nothing.
items.reference:
Signal to pattern
📖 reads far outnumber writes, shapes differ → CQRS
🕰️ state must be rebuilt from full history → event sourcing
📬 change must reach others, even if they are down → outbox
🔀 one business step across services → saga
🛡️ flaky dependency must not cascade → circuit breaker
Why: choose by the structural signal in the problem, not by which name sounds most sophisticated or which one you know best.
items.learnMore:
Symptoms are not signals

A signal describes the structure of the problem: different read and write shapes, history as the primary fact, several services in one business step. A symptom such as "the report is slow" may have a cheaper cause, so check it before reaching for a pattern.

Common mistake

Reaching for CQRS because a query is slow. A missing index is a query-tuning problem and costs far less than a second data model.
items.reflection: Pick a decision you made recently because a solution "sounded right". What structural signal in the problem would have confirmed or contradicted it?

items.prompt: Support staff occasionally need to see what changed on a ticket last week. Which approach is proportionate?
choices: Full event sourcing, since history is always the primary fact
CQRS, since support reads differ from the writes
A saga, since several records are touched by an edit
A history table, since looking backward is only occasional
items.explanation: Event sourcing fits when state must always be provably rebuilt from history. "Sometimes look backward" is a lighter signal.

items.prompt: Both event sourcing and the outbox involve events. Which signal separates them?
choices: Outbox needs a relational database, while event sourcing never needs any storage at all
Outbox delivers a change to others; event sourcing derives state from history
Event sourcing delivers faster than the outbox does
They are one pattern that goes by two different names
items.explanation: One answers "tell others reliably", the other answers "the present must be rebuildable from the past". They can coexist.

items.prompt: A problem seems to match two rows of the signals table. What does the unit suggest?
choices: Choose whichever row has the more advanced-sounding name or the shorter diagram
Implement both patterns in full just to be safe
Re-check the signals, since many problems match more than one row
Pick the row that you have personally used before
items.explanation: Overlap is normal. Re-reading the structural signals decides which row, or combination, genuinely applies.

items.prompt: Why does choosing the right catalog entry not finish the design?
choices: It is usually wrong for complex real-world production systems
It describes a class of problems, not your constraints
It only works when copied without any changes
items.explanation: The entry gives the shape and trade-offs; retention, scope and similar decisions remain yours.

items.prompt: After choosing event sourcing for compliance, which decision is still open?
choices: Whether any history exists in the first place
Whether state comes from events
How long the history is retained
items.explanation: Retention is a constraint-specific choice that the pattern leaves to you.

items.prompt: Is the catalog entry the start or the finish of the design?
choices: The finish, once everyone agrees on the name
The start; the real design talk follows
Neither, entries are not for design
items.explanation: It hands you a structure and trade-offs, and the real design conversation follows.

items.prompt: What does a reference architecture hand you?
choices: A finished design that is ready to deploy
A guarantee that no decisions are left
A starting structure and known trade-offs
items.explanation: It saves rediscovery, but it does not decide your constraints for you.

items.prompt: What is the most common misuse of a catalog, according to L2?
choices: Treating the pattern name as the finish line
Reading the catalog before starting a design
Adapting the pattern to the local constraints
items.explanation: Teams borrow the label to justify a design without doing the adaptation work.

items.prompt: Where does a saga's value actually live?
choices: In the particular order in which the services are called
In the name of the pattern used in the docs
In the compensating action for each forward step
items.explanation: Without compensating actions, a saga is just a sequence of calls with no way to undo a partial failure.

items.prompt: Another decision left after choosing event sourcing is which fields to record as events. Why?
choices: Perhaps only the regulated fields need history
The pattern forbids recording any field at all, ever
Every field is always recorded the same way
items.explanation: Scope is a constraint-specific choice; recording everything may cost more than the requirement demands.

items.prompt: Do you have to buy anything to use the public pattern catalogs?
choices: Yes, each single entry needs its own paid licence before you can read it
No, they are free; the value is in the written failure modes
Only the cloud provider entries are free to read
items.explanation: The value is that someone already wrote down the failure modes so you do not rediscover them.

items.prompt: A team ships a saga for checkout with no compensating action for a failed step. What did they adopt?
choices: A correct saga that has weak logging
A circuit breaker under another name
The name of the pattern, without its mechanism
The whole pattern, minus a few optional extras
items.explanation: A saga's whole value is the undo paired with each step. Without it, partial failure leaves the system inconsistent.
items.reference:
Pattern name is the start
🧭 Catalog gives: shape, known trade-offs, a diagram
🛠️ You still decide: retention, scope, caching, how often to poll
⚠️ Copying only the label leaves partial failure unhandled
Why: a catalog entry describes a class of problems, so your own constraints still need decisions after the pattern is chosen.
items.learnMore:
Starting structure, not finished design

Even with event sourcing correctly chosen, the team still decides how long history is kept, whether every field or only regulated ones are event-sourced, and how read models rebuild. The entry supplies the structure and the trade-offs; the constraints are yours.

Common mistake

Treating the pattern name as the finish line of the design conversation, instead of its start.
items.reflection: Think of a recipe or template you followed exactly once and had to adjust the next time. Which parts were the "class of problem" and which were your constraints?

items.prompt: Event sourcing is the right entry for a compliance system. Which question does the catalog entry not answer for them?

Whether state can be rebuilt from the events
Whether past facts get overwritten by new ones
How long this team must keep its history
items.explanation: The first three are the pattern itself. Retention depends on this team's own regulatory requirement.

Adaptation, so long as the mechanism stays intact
A violation of the catalog entry's own rules
A mistake, since catalog entries cannot be adjusted
items.explanation: Changing a constraint-specific parameter is the expected adaptation step. The mechanism is what must not be dropped.

items.prompt: A fit check compares which two things?
choices: The system's constraints and the pattern's assumptions
The pattern's name and the team's past experience with it
The number of boxes in two competing diagrams
items.explanation: The step that a rushed adoption skips is confirming the pattern was designed for the constraints you actually have.

items.prompt: In the outbox pattern, when is the event written?
choices: After the state change committed
In the same transaction as the state change
Only when the publisher happens to poll next
items.explanation: The same-transaction write is what makes both succeed or both roll back.

items.prompt: Why does the outbox fit a consumer that is offline for hours?
choices: Consumers pull from a durable log at their own pace
Consumers are called live and must answer quickly each time
Offline consumers are removed from the system
items.explanation: Rows wait in the outbox until acknowledged, so an outage delays notifications rather than losing them.

items.prompt: What does the 6-month replay requirement turn into under the pattern?
choices: A full redesign of the whole order service and its schema
A retention policy decision, not a redesign
A rule that every event is deleted at once
items.explanation: Log retention is a configuration choice, so the requirement still fits the pattern.

items.prompt: Only 3 consumers exist, and the pattern scales to many. Is that a reason to reject it?
choices: Yes, spare capacity always counts against the fit
Yes, unless a fourth is planned
No, it is over-provisioned but still a fit
items.explanation: Spare scalability does not contradict any constraint, so it is not a mismatch.

items.prompt: Why did the team choose a short polling interval over a message broker?
choices: A broker cannot deliver to three consumers at once
Polling was cheap and simple for 3 known consumers
Polling is always faster than any message broker
items.explanation: A broker would add operational surface that three known consumers did not justify.

items.prompt: Why did the team skip a full CQRS read-model layer?
choices: CQRS cannot be combined with an outbox at all in practice
Auditors forbid every separate read model
The system lacks different read and write shapes
items.explanation: The CQRS signal was absent, so adding it would solve a problem the system lacks.

items.prompt: In the interactive demo, what happens to hours saved as match quality drops toward "poor fit"?
choices: The hours saved shrink toward zero
The hours saved grow, since more design is needed
The hours saved stay the same
items.explanation: The saving comes from design work the pattern removes, and a poor fit removes little of it.

items.prompt: A team needs consumers updated within 50 ms and cannot tolerate silent misses. What should they check first?
choices: Whether the pattern has a well-known and famous name
Whether poll-based delivery matches their latency and guarantees
Whether the pattern has a well-known and famous name in the industry
Whether three consumers is the right number to support
items.explanation: The outbox walkthrough fit "eventually, replayable". A very different latency profile is a mismatch the fit table exists to catch.
items.reference:
Fit check
✅ Never lost mid-crash ↔ event written in the same transaction
✅ Consumer down for hours ↔ pull from a durable log at its own pace
✅ Six-month replay ↔ retention is a config choice
❓ Strict latency or "consumer never returns" ↔ not in the assumptions
Why: adopt a pattern only when its assumptions hold for your constraints; a matching name is not evidence.

items.prompt: What property makes the transactional outbox work?
choices: The event is written in the same transaction as the change
The event is sent twice, just for extra safety against any loss
The event is written later by a separate team
items.explanation: Atomic commit of both writes removes the window where a crash loses the event.

items.prompt: A team has an outbox table but inserts the event after the update commits. What is missing?
choices: The retention policy for old rows
The atomicity guarantee
The consumer list
items.explanation: Two separate calls reintroduce the very gap the pattern was meant to close.

items.prompt: A crash happens between the update commit and the separate event insert. What is the result?
choices: The event is silently lost
The event gets delivered twice to consumers
The update is undone
items.explanation: The state changed but nothing recorded it, so consumers never hear about it.

items.prompt: A "CQRS" read model is a cache updated synchronously from the write model. What is it really?
choices: Plain CQRS
Caching with extra steps
An event-sourced store built on stored history
items.explanation: The separation of read and write concerns is missing, so only the caching effect is present.

items.prompt: A saga has no compensating action for a failed step. What follows when step three fails?
choices: Earlier steps undo themselves without any help from you
Step three is retried forever at no cost
Earlier steps stay applied and the data is inconsistent
items.explanation: Without undo steps, a partial failure leaves earlier work in place.

items.prompt: What does CQRS actually separate?
choices: Two copies of one table kept in lockstep by a trigger
A read model shaped for queries from a write model
Two teams that work on a single service
items.explanation: The point is structurally different models, not duplication.

items.prompt: What goes wrong if the publisher calls subscribers inside the order transaction?
choices: Orders can never be updated again after the first failure
Events are delivered before they even exist
A slow consumer can block or fail the order update
items.explanation: The decoupling between "state is durable" and "everyone acknowledged" is lost.

items.prompt: What is cargo-cult adoption of a pattern?
choices: Copying the name and diagram but skipping the key property
Adapting a pattern to your local constraints
Reading a catalog carefully before starting any design work
items.explanation: The ritual is present but the mechanism that produces the benefit is not.

items.prompt: Which symptom shows a team skipped the outbox's key property?
choices: The outbox table has a unique index on its generated id column
The event insert is a separate call after the update commits
The publisher polls on a fixed repeating schedule
Consumers acknowledge each notification they receive
items.explanation: The other items are ordinary operation. Only a separate, later insert breaks the atomic write.
items.reference:
Name versus mechanism
🏷️ "Outbox table" but event inserted after commit → atomicity skipped
🏷️ "CQRS" but read model is a synchronous cache → caching, not CQRS
🏷️ "Saga" with no undo step → partial failure unhandled
Why: the pattern works because of one property; copying the diagram without that property gives the cost without the benefit.
items.learnMore:
Find the one property that makes it work

Each pattern has a mechanism you can name in a sentence: outbox writes the event in the same transaction, CQRS separates the read model from the write model, saga pairs every step with an undo. If you cannot point to that property in the system, you adopted the name only.

Common mistake

Believing that having the table, the label or the diagram means the pattern is in place.
items.reflection: Choose a practice at your workplace that goes by a famous name. What is the one property that makes it work, and could someone follow the ritual while skipping it?

items.prompt: A team calls its synchronously updated read cache "CQRS". Which diagnosis is right?
choices: It is CQRS, because reads and writes use different code
It is event sourcing, because the cache updates on write
The read side is not separate, so it is just a cache
It is a saga, because two steps run in a fixed order
items.explanation: CQRS needs a read model shaped independently for its queries. A mirror updated in lockstep adds only caching.

items.prompt: The order service calls billing directly inside its own transaction. Which outbox property is lost?

items.explanation: A slow or down billing service would now delay or fail the order update, so outages stop being merely delays.

items.prompt: A booking saga has no undo for step two. Which change restores the mechanism?
choices: Add detailed logging to every single call between the services
Pair every forward step with a matching compensating step
Retry the failed step many more times
Run the steps in a noticeably faster order
items.explanation: Logging and retries do not undo earlier effects. Compensation is the property that makes partial failure recoverable.
